title: Reinterpreting Dave Brubeck's tunes: Kathy's Waltz, democracy and rock influence
summary: Dan and Chris describe giving their father's pieces new feels such as reggae, the quartet's democratic process and their rock and roll generational influence.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we are at the morning after with Dan and Chris Brubeck, who played a marvelous concert in Wellin Hall at Hamilton College last night. I was enthralled by the interpretations of your father’s music. The core of them were there but how do you decide to bring them alive so that they fit the way you play?

I think you know certain things, I’ll hear other ways to play something like for instance in “Kathy’s Waltz,” I’ve always heard that that could be a great kind of reggae-feeling thing, which you wouldn’t think of right away but we tried it and it was like hey that actually works great. And I remember at the recording session Mike had worked out this whole opening thing and it was like, “Oh yeah, that works great but I’d really like to play a chordal guitar thing.” And it was like, “Well do that in the beginning and then we’ll go into it,” which is how we wound up doing it. But a lot of times everyone’s got their individual, like, ideas, and we just throw them out and you know with my dad’s music I kind of know it inside out. So for years all that stuff rattles around and you hear it in different ways. And so many of his tunes I’ll be practicing and I’ll think oh you could do this with that, and I’ll just approach it completely differently, slightly for my own sanity but you know also just because you can interpret things so many different ways and it’s good because later you can use that even if you’re not playing that particular style you can use that in terms of what you add to a piece, you know, how you approach it one night thing.

The other thing just in general is that the pianist in our group, Chuck Lamb, and a guitarist, Mike DeMicco and Dan and I, it’s a highly democratic process you know. So when we put out a record or when we do a concert, it is sort of like a Venn diagram of all the things that we happen to think is cool, probably much to our commercial demise you know, well in terms of like for example none of us wants to make a record that sounds anything like any Kenny G record. Sorry, Kenny. Or any of the hundreds of sax players that all sound the same to me that are sort of smooth jazz you know people or whatever. There’s this thing that Chuck thinks is cool, Mike thinks is cool, we think it’s cool, and that’s narrowly where we go. But you know like when Dan was mentioning reggae, like

for “Kathy’s Waltz” it’s just interesting to think of when “Kathy’s Waltz” was written reggae didn’t even exist. You know? So because our dad went out to the Middle East and he incorporated music that didn’t exist in the United States like the Turkish beat that became “Blue Rondo” I feel like he sort of gave us the grand rights to explore and put other music into our re-interpretations of his music. If he were our age he’d be doing it. And the other thing is because of our age we all have a rock & roll kind of influence, even though we’re not playing rock & roll. Like I try to explain to people, like I said, “Well Dan is a really interesting drummer, I mean he’s quite amazing, but think if Keith Moon played jazz.” You know? Because there’s a different energy approach. And then Mike can do all the rock & roll stuff and Chuck is very percussive. So we all respect and like, you know, straight ahead bebop and all that kind of stuff. But we can’t change what’s crept into us culturally because of the age we are, and I know conversely in doing gigs with Dave and Gerry Mulligan and different people, they can’t authentically incorporate any of that rock & roll language into what they’re doing.
Yeah, I’ve heard that like you’re still playing straight eighth notes. Like with the older fellas like in a big band. And you give them a rock number and they’re still swinging.
Yeah, they all sound like Herman Munster.
Not all. I mean there are some exceptions. But mainly I’m just acknowledging that each generation has their cultural influences that are in their blood.
